summary: This FYI memo answers the question what is the Internet, and was produced by the User Services Working Group of the IETF. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo explains the Internet as a group of connected networks, people and shared resources. It describes how the network grew and how its component organizations handled standards, funding and operations in 1993.

questions: fyi on what is the internet
subtitle: A 1993 overview of the Internet's history, organization, funding and open questions.

tldr.problem: The memo notes that there is no single short definition of the Internet because it includes networks, protocols, users and shared resources.
tldr.mechanism: It presents several ways to describe the Internet and reviews its history, network structure, administration, funding and issues as understood in 1993.
tldr.outcome: The memo is an Informational snapshot from 1993; its account of growth, governance and future questions reflects that period.

today: RFC 1462 is an Informational memo published in May 1993, and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its description of Internet organizations and open issues is a snapshot from that time.

sections.title: Several Ways to Define the Internet
sections.content:
The memo says there is no single agreed definition of the Internet. It can mean networks that use common protocols, the physical routers and circuits that connect them, the people who use and develop them, or the resources reachable through them.

It describes the Internet as having grown from a U.S. Department of Defense experiment. The connected networks shared protocols, while gateways also connected networks and services that used other protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet is not one network owned by one organization. It is a changing collection of connected networks, people and resources.

sections.title: From Research Network to Connected Networks
sections.content:
The memo traces the Internet's beginnings to efforts to connect the ARPAnet with radio and satellite networks. The ARPAnet assumed parts of the network could fail, so communicating computers had responsibility for completing communication. They sent data in Internet Protocol (IP) packets.

As local networks and workstations spread, organizations wanted to connect whole networks. The National Science Foundation built NSFNET to link supercomputer centers and regional networks. The memo says its first lines ran at 56,000 bits per second and that a 1987 upgrade used lines faster by a factor of 20.
sections.plainLanguage: Researchers connected separate networks so computers could communicate across them. As use grew, organizations expanded the network and upgraded its links.

sections.title: Networks and Gateways
sections.content:
The memo describes the Internet as a collection of networks using IP that cooperate to provide connectivity. It also notes that networks using other protocols, such as Bitnet and DECnet, connected through gateways. Some gateways initially transferred electronic mail and later translated other services.

The memo treats the boundary of the Internet as a matter of participation as well as technology: it says whether another network is part of the Internet may depend on whether it considers itself part of it. The definition can change as networks connect or disconnect.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks using different rules can connect through gateways. The memo says the Internet's boundaries can change as networks choose to participate.

sections.title: Standards, Administration and Funding
sections.content:
The memo says the Internet has no single president or authority figure. It describes the Internet Society as appointing the Internet Architecture Board, which provides technical direction and oversees standards and unique numbers. The Internet Engineering Task Force discusses operational and near-term technical issues and forms working groups; their reports may be documentation, voluntary practices or proposals for standards.

No one pays for the Internet as a whole. Organizations pay for their own networks and connections, and network operations centers coordinate with one another when problems arise. The memo presents each network as responsible for its own part of the connected system.
sections.plainLanguage: Different groups manage different parts of the Internet and cooperate on shared technical rules. Each organization pays for its own network connections.

sections.title: Issues the Memo Saw in 1993
sections.content:
The memo discusses international growth, commercialization and privatization as open issues. It reports that the Internet reached more than 50 countries and that about 25% of connected hosts were in Europe. It also describes limited telephone infrastructure as a constraint in some regions.

It says restrictions on commercial use were under review and discusses proposals for private companies to provide Internet connections. The memo describes questions about funding existing connections, including those used by schools. These observations are the authors' view of the issues in 1993, not a statement about later developments.
sections.plainLanguage: In 1993, the memo described international growth and business use as developing issues. It also raised questions about who would fund connections as networks changed hands.
